title: Kansas police chief used Flock license plate cameras 164 times to track ex-girlfriend

reading.body:
This is insider misuse of a deployed surveillance system, not a failure of the software's accuracy. A license plate reader network built to let police check vehicles against investigative interest was queried by the official who controlled access to it, repeatedly, against people he knew personally. The failure sits at the point where a legitimate tool meets an authorised user with no second party between the query and the result.

Catching it would have required reviewing query logs against case records, since the pattern was repeated lookups of the same few people over months rather than one anomalous search. A requirement that each lookup be tied to an open case, or that repeated checks on the same plate be approved by someone else, would have surfaced the behaviour while it was happening. The physical following in a police vehicle is a separate act that no query control would have caught.

What is not established is the precise number of lookups: the headline reports 164 and the summary of the certification order reports 228, and the given material does not reconcile them. The account rests on a certification order and a single outlet's reporting, and the order is a finding against his certification, not a criminal verdict.

reports.title: Kansas police chief used Flock license plate cameras 164 times to track ex-girlfriend

summary: From June to October 2023, Sedgwick, Kansas, Police Chief Lee Nygaard reportedly used Flock Safety license plate readers 228 times to check where his ex-girlfriend and her new boyfriend were, according to a Kansas certification order. The order said he also followed them in a police vehicle and admitted jealousy influenced his actions. Nygaard resigned in October 2023 and later lost his police certification.
